Introduction to Causal ML in R

R
Causal ML
Machine Learning
Published

June 6, 2026

Machine learning is very good at prediction. It can tell us who is likely to churn, which loan may default, or which student may score poorly on an exam. But many real decisions are not prediction questions. They are intervention questions.

Suppose you are deciding whether to offer tutoring to a student. The real question is not “Who tends to score well?” The real question is “How much would this student’s score change if they received tutoring?”

That is a causal question.

Prediction Is Not Causation

If we look at historical data, we may notice that students who received tutoring scored lower on average than students who did not. A predictive model could learn that tutoring is associated with lower scores.

That does not mean tutoring hurts students.

It may simply be that struggling students were more likely to receive tutoring in the first place. This is called confounding. A confounder is a variable that affects both treatment assignment and the outcome.

In this example:

  • Students with low baseline scores may be more likely to get tutoring.
  • Those same students may also have lower future scores, even after extra help.

So the raw comparison is unfair.

What Causal ML Tries to Estimate

The central idea in causal inference is the counterfactual.

For each person, we want to compare two worlds:

  • What would happen if they received the treatment?
  • What would happen if they did not?

Of course, we only get to observe one of those worlds. Causal methods try to recover the missing one as carefully as possible.

At a high level, causal ML combines two ideas:

  • Causal inference gives the framework for asking intervention questions correctly.
  • Machine learning helps model complex patterns, especially when treatment effects are not the same for everyone.

Why Causal ML Is Needed

Classical causal tools such as randomized experiments and regression are extremely important. But modern decision problems are often more complicated:

  • There may be many confounding variables.
  • Relationships may be non-linear.
  • The treatment may help some people much more than others.
  • We may want to personalize decisions rather than estimate one average effect.

Causal ML is useful when we want to estimate effects like:

  • Which customers will respond most to a marketing offer?
  • Which patients benefit most from a treatment?
  • Which students gain most from tutoring?

The key point is simple: standard ML predicts outcomes, while causal ML tries to estimate the effect of an action.

A Simple Example in R

We will simulate data for a tutoring program. In our synthetic world:

  • students have a baseline test score,
  • students study for different numbers of hours,
  • some students are more motivated than others,
  • weaker students are more likely to receive tutoring,
  • tutoring helps, but it helps weaker students more.

This setup is useful because we know the true treatment effect in the simulated data. That lets us compare naive analysis with better causal analysis.

set.seed(42)

n <- 1500

students <- data.frame(
  pretest = pmin(100, pmax(30, round(rnorm(n, mean = 68, sd = 12)))),
  study_hours = pmax(0, round(rnorm(n, mean = 6, sd = 2), 1)),
  motivation = runif(n, min = 0, max = 1)
)

# Students with lower pretest scores are more likely to be assigned tutoring.
log_odds_treat <- 2.5 - 0.04 * students$pretest + 0.8 * students$motivation
prob_treat <- plogis(log_odds_treat)
students$treat <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = prob_treat)

# True treatment effect is larger for weaker students.
students$true_tau <- 12 - 0.10 * students$pretest + 2 * students$motivation

students$posttest <- 35 +
  0.55 * students$pretest +
  1.8 * students$study_hours +
  6 * students$motivation +
  students$treat * students$true_tau +
  rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 5)

head(students)
  pretest study_hours motivation treat true_tau posttest
1      84         4.8 0.24646324     1 4.092926 94.39913
2      61         5.7 0.53030519     1 6.960610 82.88053
3      72         4.0 0.21397210     0 5.227944 82.98620
4      76         7.7 0.02584904     0 4.451698 87.04493
5      73         4.4 0.34200247     0 5.384005 91.06745
6      67         6.7 0.39413527     1 6.088271 99.91392

Step 1: The Naive Comparison

Let us compare average post-test scores for tutored and non-tutored students.

tapply(students$posttest, students$treat, mean)
       0        1 
87.10406 91.76007 
naive_effect <- with(students,
  mean(posttest[treat == 1]) - mean(posttest[treat == 0])
)

naive_effect
[1] 4.656002

This difference is easy to compute, but it mixes together two things:

  • the effect of tutoring,
  • the fact that struggling students were more likely to receive tutoring.

Now compare the baseline scores of the two groups.

tapply(students$pretest, students$treat, mean)
       0        1 
70.46565 65.40473

If the tutored group starts from a weaker baseline, then a raw comparison is not an apples-to-apples comparison.

Step 2: What Is the True Average Effect?

Because we simulated the data, we actually know the true treatment effect for each student.

true_ate <- mean(students$true_tau)
true_ate
[1] 6.228336

In real life, we do not know this number. But in a simulation it is a helpful benchmark.

Step 3: A Simple Regression Adjustment

A first causal step is to adjust for observed confounders. This is not yet “causal ML” in the modern sense, but it is an important baseline.

lm_fit <- lm(posttest ~ treat + pretest + study_hours + motivation, data = students)
summary(lm_fit)$coefficients
              Estimate Std. Error  t value      Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 37.7458376 0.92990797 40.59094 1.873577e-243
treat        6.4573821 0.27542075 23.44552 8.890104e-104
pretest      0.4925642 0.01146321 42.96915 2.269745e-263
study_hours  1.8766798 0.06490833 28.91277 2.240400e-146
motivation   7.5710141 0.45894933 16.49641  2.691824e-56

The coefficient on treat is now comparing students with similar baseline characteristics instead of mixing everyone together.

Step 4: A Simple Causal ML Idea

One common idea in causal ML is to estimate two models:

  • one model for the treated group,
  • one model for the control group.

Then for each student we predict:

  • expected score if treated,
  • expected score if not treated,

and subtract the two predictions. This is sometimes called a T-learner.

We will use decision trees to keep the code approachable.

library(rpart)

treated_model <- rpart(
  posttest ~ pretest + study_hours + motivation,
  data = students[students$treat == 1, ],
  method = "anova",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01, minsplit = 30)
)

control_model <- rpart(
  posttest ~ pretest + study_hours + motivation,
  data = students[students$treat == 0, ],
  method = "anova",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01, minsplit = 30)
)

students$mu1_hat <- predict(treated_model, newdata = students)
students$mu0_hat <- predict(control_model, newdata = students)
students$tau_hat <- students$mu1_hat - students$mu0_hat

head(students[, c("pretest", "motivation", "true_tau", "tau_hat")])
  pretest motivation true_tau   tau_hat
1      84 0.24646324 4.092926  6.132321
2      61 0.53030519 6.960610 10.674708
3      72 0.21397210 5.227944  3.464018
4      76 0.02584904 4.451698  2.585313
5      73 0.34200247 5.384005  6.132321
6      67 0.39413527 6.088271  6.453480

This gives an estimated treatment effect for each student, not just one overall average.

Who Benefits the Most?

Now let us look at estimated treatment effects by baseline score band.

students$score_band <- cut(
  students$pretest,
  breaks = c(30, 50, 65, 80, 100),
  include.lowest = TRUE
)

aggregate(cbind(true_tau, tau_hat) ~ score_band, data = students, mean)
  score_band true_tau  tau_hat
1    [30,50] 8.486052 7.586667
2    (50,65] 7.053347 6.644504
3    (65,80] 5.766436 7.026083
4   (80,100] 4.347571 5.490518

You should see a pattern where lower-scoring students tend to benefit more from tutoring. That is called heterogeneous treatment effects. In many real applications, this is exactly what decision-makers want to know.

Visualizing Estimated Effects

plot(
  students$pretest,
  students$tau_hat,
  pch = 16,
  col = rgb(0.1, 0.4, 0.7, 0.25),
  xlab = "Pre-test score",
  ylab = "Estimated tutoring effect",
  main = "Estimated Treatment Effect by Baseline Score"
)

lines(
  lowess(students$pretest, students$tau_hat, f = 0.4),
  col = "firebrick",
  lwd = 3
)

The smooth line helps show how the estimated effect changes across students. In this simulation, the estimated effect should generally decline as the pre-test score rises.

Why This Is Still Only a Starting Point

This example is useful for intuition, but real causal ML is more careful than this simple workflow.

In practice, analysts often use methods such as:

  • causal forests,
  • doubly robust learners,
  • meta-learners such as the T-learner, S-learner, and X-learner,
  • uplift models for treatment targeting.

They also worry about assumptions such as:

  • no important unobserved confounders,
  • enough overlap between treated and untreated groups,
  • correct measurement of treatment and outcome.

No algorithm can fully fix bad data or a broken study design.

A Few Takeaways

  • Causal questions ask what would happen under different actions.
  • Predictive ML alone cannot answer causal questions.
  • Confounding can make naive comparisons misleading.
  • Causal ML is especially useful when treatment effects vary across people.
  • In R, even a simple simulation can help build intuition for counterfactual thinking.

One More Useful Check

Since this is simulated data, we can compare the average estimated effect with the true average effect.

c(
  naive = naive_effect,
  regression_adjusted = coef(lm_fit)["treat"],
  t_learner_average = mean(students$tau_hat),
  true_ate = true_ate
)
                    naive regression_adjusted.treat         t_learner_average 
                 4.656002                  6.457382                  6.719138 
                 true_ate 
                 6.228336

This comparison is a nice reminder that causal estimation is about recovering the effect of an intervention, not just finding correlations in the observed data.

If you want to extend this example, try changing the data-generating process:

  • make treatment almost random,
  • add stronger confounding,
  • make the treatment effect non-linear,
  • remove one important confounder and see what happens.

That kind of experimentation is one of the fastest ways to develop intuition for causal ML.
